original_question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have a non-trivial infinite-dimensional separable quotient?
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact open problem stated in the paper almost verbatim: it has the correct universal quantifier (every), the correct ambient class (infinite-dimensional Banach spaces), and the correct conclusion (existence of a non-trivial infinite-dimensional separable quotient).
missing_details: To make the question fully stand-alone, introduce the ambient space explicitly as a Banach space X.
Clarify that a quotient means a Banach quotient X/Y by a closed linear subspace Y of X.
Make explicit that there are no extra hypotheses on X in the problem itself (for example, no separability, reflexivity, basis, or dual assumptions).

The paper retains the adjective "non-trivial," but once the quotient is required to be infinite-dimensional, that adjective is logically redundant; a stand-alone version can simply require the quotient to be separable and infinite-dimensional.
To stay paper-faithful, do not strengthen the conclusion to "has a Schauder basis"; that is the older neighboring Problem 14, not Problem 15.
The scalar field is left implicit in the printed problem statement, so a stand-alone rewrite may either keep the standard Banach-space convention implicit or spell it out separately.
refined_question: For every infinite-dimensional Banach space X, does there exist a closed linear subspace Y of X such that the quotient Banach space X/Y is separable and infinite-dimensional?
justification: The draft is targeting exactly the paper's Section 10 separable quotient problem. In that section, the authors first state the older Banach-Pelczynski question as Problem 14, asking whether every infinite-dimensional Banach space has an infinite-dimensional quotient with a Schauder basis. They then cite Theorem 13, which gives this for every infinite-dimensional separable space, and immediately say that the problem "now becomes" Problem 15, namely the separable quotient problem. Your draft matches that Problem 15 essentially word for word, so the correct refinement is only to make the quotient notation explicit and keep the scope narrow. The later results in Theorems 14 and 15 are partial positive cases, not reformulations of the target question.
